newsitem.title: USA: White House unfazed by reported budget defection.
newsitem.headline: White House unfazed by reported budget defection.

text.p: The White House on Tuesday took a philosophical view of House Democratic leader Richard Gephardt's reported plan to oppose President Bill Clinton's budget deal with congressional Republicans.

"We've got a lot of Democrats and a lot of Republicans in support of the budget agreement, and we understand and respect those with divergent views," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said as reports spread through the U.S. capital that Gephardt was deserting Clinton on the budget issue.

Gephardt, a potential rival to Vice President Al Gore for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2000, reportedly planned to announce his position at a news conference later in the day. His spokesman was unavailable for comment.
The Missouri Democrat has "strong feelings on that (agreement) and we respect his strong feelings," McCurry said.

The agreement would balance the budget by cutting spending by $304 billion over the next five years below what would have occurred without changes in policy. Much of this comes from almost $130 billion in savings from Medicare and Medicaid.
The deal also provides for a net $85 billion tax cut by 2002 and gives Clinton $33 billion for domestic goals.
Asked if Gephardt had told the White House of his intention to buck Clinton on the budget, McCurry replied: "I think we've got a pretty good sense of what he's thinking and feeling."

Gephardt's reported defection inevitably evoked memories of Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich's 1990 stand on a budget agreement between then-President George Bush and the Democrats then in control of Congress.
Although Gingrich was a back-bencher at the time, he was able to sink the deal and embarrass Bush by forging a unusual coalition of conservative Republicans and liberal Democrats.
McCurry said he saw no resemblance between then and now.
"Two entirely different situations. Two entirely different moments in history. I don't see any comparison," he said.
